concept.body: Four valid parallelogram tests: (1) both pairs of opposite sides congruent; (2) both pairs of opposite angles congruent; (3) diagonals bisect EACH OTHER (mutual); (4) ONE pair of opposite sides both congruent and parallel — the same pair must do both jobs. Mixed pairs (one pair congruent, the other parallel) fails: the isosceles trapezoid is the counterexample.

explanationVariants: Same-pair congruent-and-parallel is valid test 4; the mixed version is defeated by the isosceles trapezoid.
The pair must carry BOTH jobs — that's what powers the SAS + CPCTC proof.

widget.prompt: Which is a VALID parallelogram test?

options.label: One pair of opposite sides is both congruent AND parallel
options.feedback: Test 4 — the same-pair condition. The diagonal splits it into SAS-congruent triangles, and CPCTC parallels the other pair.

options.label: One pair congruent, the other pair parallel
options.feedback: The isosceles trapezoid meets this and is no parallelogram — mixed pairs certify nothing.

options.label: One diagonal bisects the other
options.feedback: One-way bisection describes a kite. The valid test needs MUTUAL bisection.

options.label: All four sides congruent to each other's opposites... in one pair only
options.feedback: A single congruent pair alone (without its parallelism) is defeated by the isosceles trapezoid's legs.

steps.body: Chapter 2 ran one direction: IF a parallelogram, THEN properties. Now reverse the arrows. Each property has a **converse test**: show a quadrilateral has both pairs of opposite sides congruent, or both pairs of opposite angles congruent, or diagonals that bisect each other — and it MUST be a parallelogram. Properties describe; tests certify.

widget.prompt: What's the logical difference between a parallelogram PROPERTY and a parallelogram TEST?

options.label: A property flows FROM knowing it's a parallelogram; a test flows TOWARD that conclusion — converse directions
options.feedback: Same sentence, opposite arrows: property = parallelogram ⇒ fact; test = fact ⇒ parallelogram. Each converse needs its own proof.

options.label: They're identical statements
options.feedback: A statement and its converse can differ in truth — here both happen to hold, but only because each converse was separately proved.

options.label: Tests are approximate; properties are exact
options.feedback: Both are exact theorems — the difference is pure direction: describing a known parallelogram vs certifying an unknown quadrilateral.

options.label: Properties are for rectangles only
options.feedback: Chapter 2's properties covered ALL parallelograms — and each one's converse becomes a general-purpose test.

steps.body: The workhorse tests: (1) both pairs of opposite sides congruent; (2) both pairs of opposite angles congruent; (3) diagonals bisect each other; (4) **one pair of opposite sides BOTH congruent and parallel** — the one-pair shortcut. Test 4's proof: the diagonal + alternate interior angles gives SAS, then CPCTC delivers the second parallel pair.

explanationVariants: For the diagonals to bisect each other, AO must equal OC: x + 4 = 3x − 10 gives x = 7, so AO = 11.
Set the halves equal (that's the test's requirement) and solve: x = 7, AO = 7 + 4 = 11.

widget.prompt: Quadrilateral ABCD has diagonals meeting at O, with AO = x + 4 and OC = 3x − 10. For what value of AO does the diagonal-bisection test apply (given BO = OD already)?

commonErrors.feedback: 7 is x — the test needs the segment length: AO = x + 4 = 11.
22 is the full diagonal AC after the test passes. AO alone is half: 11.
3 solves x + 4 = 3x − ... incorrectly — collect terms: 14 = 2x, x = 7, AO = 11.

steps.body: One tempting shortcut FAILS: “one pair of sides congruent, and the OTHER pair parallel.” The isosceles trapezoid from Chapter 4 defeats it — parallel bases, congruent legs, and definitely not a parallelogram. Test 4 works only because the SAME pair carries both jobs. Mixed pairs certify nothing.

explanationVariants: An isosceles trapezoid has exactly that data — parallel bases, congruent legs — and only ONE parallel pair, so it's no parallelogram.
Chapter 4's isosceles trapezoid is the standing counterexample to the mixed-pairs shortcut.

widget.prompt: “One pair of opposite sides is parallel, and the OTHER pair is congruent.” Which figure proves this is NOT a valid parallelogram test?

options.label: An isosceles trapezoid
options.feedback: Parallel bases + congruent legs, yet only one parallel pair — the data holds, the conclusion fails. Counterexample complete.

options.label: A square
options.feedback: A square IS a parallelogram — it can't witness the test failing. You need a figure with the data but WITHOUT parallelogram-hood.

options.label: A kite
options.feedback: A typical kite has NO parallel sides, so it doesn't even satisfy the test's data — it can't test the implication.

options.label: There is none — the test is valid
options.feedback: The isosceles trapezoid defeats it: bases parallel, legs congruent, not a parallelogram. Same-pair is what makes test 4 work.

explanationVariants: Both diagonal-bisection (test 3) and same-pair congruent-and-parallel (test 4) certify; the mixed-pair claim does not.
Valid: tests 3 and 4. Invalid: the isosceles-trapezoid-shaped shortcut.

widget.prompt: Which single fact about quadrilateral PQRS certifies it is a parallelogram?

options.label: PQ ≅ SR and PQ ∥ SR (the same pair, both jobs)
options.feedback: Test 4: one pair doing double duty. The diagonal + SAS + CPCTC proof makes the other pair parallel for free.

options.label: PQ ≅ SR and PS ∥ QR (mixed pairs)
options.feedback: Mixed pairs is the isosceles-trapezoid trap — congruent legs with the OTHER pair parallel certifies nothing.

options.label: Diagonal PR bisects diagonal QS (one-way)
options.feedback: One-way bisection is a KITE behavior — the test needs MUTUAL bisection, each diagonal cutting the other in half.

options.label: One pair of congruent angles
options.feedback: The angle test needs BOTH pairs of opposite angles congruent — a single pair leaves the shape loose.

widget.prompt: The jig's two rods are the diagonals: equal in length, crossing at their midpoints. Inspect midpoints and distances, and move D until both conditions hold at once.
widget.successFeedback: A rectangle — and no coordinates were needed to predict it. Mutual bisection alone forces a parallelogram; adding equal diagonals is the extra condition that squares the corners. The jig holds those two facts in hardware, so the elastic has no other shape available to it.
widget.positionFeedback: D is not at (1, 5) yet. Check which condition is failing: if the midpoint dots are apart the rods are not crossing at their centres, and if the side lengths disagree the elastic is not even closing a parallelogram.
widget.evidenceFeedback: Inspect both midpoints AND distances, and move D a few times first. Either fact alone is too weak — bisection without equal diagonals gives a slanted parallelogram, and this claim needs both.

predict.prompt: Two rods of EQUAL length are pinned so they cross at each other's exact midpoints. Elastic joins the four ends. The shape is always…

options.label: Any parallelogram — it depends on the crossing angle

predict.reveal: Always a rectangle. Crossing at the midpoints makes it a parallelogram; the rods being equal makes the diagonals congruent, and a parallelogram with congruent diagonals is a rectangle. The crossing angle changes how long and thin it is, never whether the corners are square.

hints: The builder has one pair congruent and the OTHER pair parallel — the invalid mix.
The cheapest valid upgrade keeps what's known and completes a real test.
Which single measurement converts the data into test 1, 3, or 4?
explanationVariants: Showing the PARALLEL pair is also congruent completes test 4 (same pair, both jobs) — one measurement.
Alternatively the other diagonal check would work, but measuring the parallel pair's lengths is the single-step repair.

widget.prompt: A builder knows: AB ≅ CD, and AD ∥ BC. Which ONE additional measurement certifies a parallelogram?

options.label: Show AD ≅ BC — then the parallel pair is also congruent (test 4)
options.feedback: Now AD carries both jobs: congruent AND parallel. One clean measurement upgrades the invalid mix into a valid certificate.

options.label: Show AB ∥ AD
options.feedback: AB and AD are CONSECUTIVE sides — in a parallelogram they're never parallel (they meet at a vertex). That would break the shape, not certify it.

options.label: Measure one diagonal's length
options.feedback: A single diagonal length certifies nothing — the diagonal test needs both diagonals CUT AT MIDPOINTS, a different setup.

options.label: No single measurement can ever suffice
options.feedback: One does: AD ≅ BC turns the parallel pair into a congruent-AND-parallel pair — test 4 fires immediately.

takeaways: Tests: both side pairs ≅, both angle pairs ≅, diagonals mutually bisect, or ONE pair both ≅ and ∥.
The mixed-pairs shortcut fails — the isosceles trapezoid is the standing counterexample.
Equal rods crossing at midpoints = rectangle: tests stack with ch3 upgrades.
